## Where to Stay in Athens

On our recent trip to Athens, we stayed at two places: a holiday apartment for two nights and a hotel for one night. I highly recommend both, which are in neighborhoods convenient for sightseeing in Athens.

#### Karma Apartments

Steps from the lively Plaka district on a quiet side street, [Karma Apartments](https://www.booking.com/hotel/gr/karma-athens-ii.en.html?aid=1905655&no_rooms=1&group_adults=2) is a real find in Athens. The one-bedroom apartment on the top floor of a building containing other holiday rentals includes a large terrace with a peek-a-boo view of the Acropolis.

#### Hotel Lozenge

On our last night in Greece, we stayed at the [Hotel Lozenge](https://www.booking.com/hotel/gr/lozenge.en.html?aid=1905655&no_rooms=1&group_adults=2) in the upscale Kolonaki neighbourhood. This is a great choice for a business-style hotel with comfortable rooms, an adjacent restaurant, and very helpful staff.

# Greek Archaeological Treasures: The “Mask of Agamemnon”

[Duncan Howitt-Marshall](https://www.greece-is.com/author/dhmarshall/)|March 14th, 2022

![Image 4](https://www.greece-is.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Mask-of-Agamemnon.jpg)

Gold death mask, famously known as the “Mask of Agamemnon,” found in Grave Circle A at Mycenae. Discovered in 1876 by amateur archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann, the mask is on display in Room 4 of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

Funeral& Bereavement

* * *

© Shutterstock

[Greece Is](https://www.greece-is.com/ "Greece Is")[Editor's Pick](https://www.greece-is.com/editors-pick/ "Editor's Pick")

## When discovered at Mycenae in 1876, Schliemann famously exclaimed “I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon!” But did it really belong to the legendary king?

“I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon,” boasted **Heinrich Schliemann, the famous amateur archaeologist** who first unearthed the gold funeral mask at Mycenae in 1876.

Imagine his excitement and joy as he carefully brushed away the dirt to reveal the mask, depicting the face of a bearded man, glinting in the sunlight. But did it really belong to the king of Homeric legend?

Schliemann discovered the mask, still fastened to its corpse, in **Shaft Grave V of Grave Circle A, immediately south of the Lion Gate**, the main entrance of the Bronze Age citadel in the Greek Argolid. It was one of seven death masks discovered in the same grave circle, alongside an enormous cache of gold artifacts, inlcuding ornate weapons, staffs, jewelry, and ceremonial cups.

Greece travel guides

Ever his own best publicist and exercising a blind faith in the Homeric epics, Schliemann made the extraordinary claim that he had found the remains of **Agamemnon, the legendary Mycenaean ruler**, in a telegraph to King George of Greece.

Agamemnon’s exploits as the commander-in-chief of the Greek army at Troy were immortalized in **Homer’s _Iliad_**. He was murdered upon his return from the war by Aegisthus, the lover of his wife Clytemnestra – the story of the Aeschylus’ tragic play “Agamemnon,” written in the 5th century BC.

Schliemann undoubtedly used the death mask to generate media interest in his excavations at the Bronze Age site, but it’s _extremely_ unlikely that it belonged to the Homeric hero, if indeed Agamemnon ever existed as a historical figure.

![Image 5](https://www.greece-is.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Grave-Circle-A.jpg)

Scale model of Mycenae. Grave Circle A is located to the right after the Lion Gate, the main entrance of the Bronze Age citadel.

What we do know is that Schliemann, who retired from commercial activities a multi-millionaire at the age of 36, was **a fanatical devotee of Homer, dedicating the rest of his life to proving the historicity of the _Iliad_ and the _Odyssey_**. As such, he gained a reputation for “salting” his archaeological digs with bogus artifacts or objects taken from elsewhere to back up his claims.

His first quest took him to Hissarlik in northwest Turkey, in search of **the ancient citadel of Troy**. From 1870 to 1873, his excavations, inlcuding the discovery of **a large cache of gold artifacts dubbed “Priam’s Treasure,”** brought him both international fame and notoriety in equal measure, especially among the academic elite who criticised his heavy-handed methods.

In 1874, Schliemann embarked on excavations at Mycenae, the heavily fortified center that gives its name to **the Late Bronze Age culture of mainland Greece from c. 1600 to 1200 BC**. The discovery and subsequent publication of the spectacular contents of Grave Circle A, inlcuding the so-called “Mask of Agamemnon,” sparked a global media frenzy at the time, but not everyone was convinced.

Ancient Messene tours

Created from a single sheet of gold, heated and hammered against a wooden mold, **the mask differs in style from the other death masks of Mycenae**, lending support to the theory that Schliemann may have had it manufactured and surreptitiously placed in the shaft grave as part of an elaborate hoax. Proponents of this argument state that it is the only one in three-dimensional form as opposed to flat, with cut-out ears, a finely-detailed beard and handlebar moustache, conspicuously different to how men are depicted in Mycenaean art, and the eyebrows form two arches instead of one. It is also extremely well preserved compared to the others.

![Image 6](https://www.greece-is.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Gold-Death-Mask.jpg)

One of the other funeral masks from Grave Circle A at Mycenae, also dated to the 16th century BC, but quite different in style to the so-called "Mask of Agamemnon."

So, was it just a publicity stunt? Did Schliemann really fabricate the mask? Or was he simply letting his imagination get the better of him?

Towards the end of this life, Schliemann, accepting doubts about the authenticity of the mask’s true owner, famously conceded: “So this is not Agamemnon … these are not his ornaments? All right, let’s call him Schulze.” But **he certainly made no admission of fraud**.

Instead, modern archaeological research has tentatively dated the mask to **the second half of the 16th century BC, at least 300 years _before_ the Trojan War** of _Iliad_-fame. One study even dated it as far back as 2500 BC – the Early Helladic period of mainland Greece.

The majority of scholars today agree that **the gold mask is authentically Mycenaean, an exquisite example of the early repoussé (embossing) technique**, and likely belonged to a warrior king or someone of extreme wealth and importance in early Mycenaean culture. Interestingly, death masks like the ones found at Mycenae have not been found at any other site from the Mycenaean world. As such, the mystery surrounding their origins continues.

Ancient Messene tours

The iconic “Mask of Agamemnon,” even if it didn’t belong to the Homeric king, is nevertheless an extraordinary treasure of prehistoric Greek archaeology. It can be seen **on display in Room 4 of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens**, mounted centrally with the other gold masks from Grave Circle A, amid the spectacular Collection of Mycenaean Antiquities.

# Greek Archaeological Treasures: The “Mask of Agamemnon”

[Duncan Howitt-Marshall](https://www.greece-is.com/author/dhmarshall/)|March 14th, 2022

![Image 4](https://www.greece-is.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Mask-of-Agamemnon.jpg)

Gold death mask, famously known as the “Mask of Agamemnon,” found in Grave Circle A at Mycenae. Discovered in 1876 by amateur archaeologist Heinrich Schliemann, the mask is on display in Room 4 of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens.

Funeral& Bereavement

* * *

© Shutterstock

[Greece Is](https://www.greece-is.com/ "Greece Is")[Editor's Pick](https://www.greece-is.com/editors-pick/ "Editor's Pick")

## When discovered at Mycenae in 1876, Schliemann famously exclaimed “I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon!” But did it really belong to the legendary king?

“I have gazed upon the face of Agamemnon,” boasted **Heinrich Schliemann, the famous amateur archaeologist** who first unearthed the gold funeral mask at Mycenae in 1876.

Imagine his excitement and joy as he carefully brushed away the dirt to reveal the mask, depicting the face of a bearded man, glinting in the sunlight. But did it really belong to the king of Homeric legend?

Schliemann discovered the mask, still fastened to its corpse, in **Shaft Grave V of Grave Circle A, immediately south of the Lion Gate**, the main entrance of the Bronze Age citadel in the Greek Argolid. It was one of seven death masks discovered in the same grave circle, alongside an enormous cache of gold artifacts, inlcuding ornate weapons, staffs, jewelry, and ceremonial cups.

Greece travel guides

Ever his own best publicist and exercising a blind faith in the Homeric epics, Schliemann made the extraordinary claim that he had found the remains of **Agamemnon, the legendary Mycenaean ruler**, in a telegraph to King George of Greece.

Agamemnon’s exploits as the commander-in-chief of the Greek army at Troy were immortalized in **Homer’s _Iliad_**. He was murdered upon his return from the war by Aegisthus, the lover of his wife Clytemnestra – the story of the Aeschylus’ tragic play “Agamemnon,” written in the 5th century BC.

Schliemann undoubtedly used the death mask to generate media interest in his excavations at the Bronze Age site, but it’s _extremely_ unlikely that it belonged to the Homeric hero, if indeed Agamemnon ever existed as a historical figure.

![Image 5](https://www.greece-is.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Grave-Circle-A.jpg)

Scale model of Mycenae. Grave Circle A is located to the right after the Lion Gate, the main entrance of the Bronze Age citadel.

What we do know is that Schliemann, who retired from commercial activities a multi-millionaire at the age of 36, was **a fanatical devotee of Homer, dedicating the rest of his life to proving the historicity of the _Iliad_ and the _Odyssey_**. As such, he gained a reputation for “salting” his archaeological digs with bogus artifacts or objects taken from elsewhere to back up his claims.

His first quest took him to Hissarlik in northwest Turkey, in search of **the ancient citadel of Troy**. From 1870 to 1873, his excavations, inlcuding the discovery of **a large cache of gold artifacts dubbed “Priam’s Treasure,”** brought him both international fame and notoriety in equal measure, especially among the academic elite who criticised his heavy-handed methods.

In 1874, Schliemann embarked on excavations at Mycenae, the heavily fortified center that gives its name to **the Late Bronze Age culture of mainland Greece from c. 1600 to 1200 BC**. The discovery and subsequent publication of the spectacular contents of Grave Circle A, inlcuding the so-called “Mask of Agamemnon,” sparked a global media frenzy at the time, but not everyone was convinced.

Ancient Messene tours

Created from a single sheet of gold, heated and hammered against a wooden mold, **the mask differs in style from the other death masks of Mycenae**, lending support to the theory that Schliemann may have had it manufactured and surreptitiously placed in the shaft grave as part of an elaborate hoax. Proponents of this argument state that it is the only one in three-dimensional form as opposed to flat, with cut-out ears, a finely-detailed beard and handlebar moustache, conspicuously different to how men are depicted in Mycenaean art, and the eyebrows form two arches instead of one. It is also extremely well preserved compared to the others.

![Image 6](https://www.greece-is.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/03/Gold-Death-Mask.jpg)

One of the other funeral masks from Grave Circle A at Mycenae, also dated to the 16th century BC, but quite different in style to the so-called "Mask of Agamemnon."

So, was it just a publicity stunt? Did Schliemann really fabricate the mask? Or was he simply letting his imagination get the better of him?

Towards the end of this life, Schliemann, accepting doubts about the authenticity of the mask’s true owner, famously conceded: “So this is not Agamemnon … these are not his ornaments? All right, let’s call him Schulze.” But **he certainly made no admission of fraud**.

Instead, modern archaeological research has tentatively dated the mask to **the second half of the 16th century BC, at least 300 years _before_ the Trojan War** of _Iliad_-fame. One study even dated it as far back as 2500 BC – the Early Helladic period of mainland Greece.

The majority of scholars today agree that **the gold mask is authentically Mycenaean, an exquisite example of the early repoussé (embossing) technique**, and likely belonged to a warrior king or someone of extreme wealth and importance in early Mycenaean culture. Interestingly, death masks like the ones found at Mycenae have not been found at any other site from the Mycenaean world. As such, the mystery surrounding their origins continues.

Ancient Messene tours

The iconic “Mask of Agamemnon,” even if it didn’t belong to the Homeric king, is nevertheless an extraordinary treasure of prehistoric Greek archaeology. It can be seen **on display in Room 4 of the National Archaeological Museum in Athens**, mounted centrally with the other gold masks from Grave Circle A, amid the spectacular Collection of Mycenaean Antiquities.

## What can you see inside the museum?

Six highlights stand out from the rest of the works:

Mask of Agamemnon Antikythera Mechanism Artemision Bronze Jockey of Artemision Thera frescoes

![Image 30: mask of agamemnon](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/mask-of-agamemnon.webp)

### Mask of Agamemnon

Heinrich Schliemann unearthed the gold funerary mask at Mycenae in 1876, inside Grave Circle A. It dates to **1550-1500 BC**, three centuries before the Trojan War, and most likely covered the face of a Mycenaean ruler whose identity remains unknown. Hammered from a single sheet of gold, the portrait sits at the centre of the museum's Mycenaean collection in **Room 4**.

![Image 31: antikythera mechanism](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/antikythera-mechanism.webp)

### Antikythera Mechanism

Divers recovered the geared bronze device in 1901 from a shipwreck off the island of Antikythera, and it dates between **150 and 100 BC**. Researchers consider it the earliest known analog computer: more than 30 interlocking gears tracked astronomical positions, predicted lunar phases and eclipses, and timed the cycle of athletic festivals. The main fragment and several smaller pieces sit in **Room 38**, alongside digital reconstructions that show the mechanism in motion.

_Photo: “Antikythera Mechanism - National Archaeological Museum, Athens by Joy of Museum” by_[_Joyofmuseums_](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Joyofmuseums).

![Image 32: Artemision in Bronze](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/artemision.webp)

### Artemision Bronze of Zeus or Poseidon

Fishermen hauled the **2.09-metre bronze figure** from the seabed off Cape Artemision in 1928, and it is one of the few surviving large bronzes from early Classical sculpture. Scholars still debate whether it depicts Zeus poised to hurl a thunderbolt or Poseidon brandishing a trident, since the original attribute did not survive. The balanced stance, anatomical precision, and outstretched arms anchor **Room 15**.

_Photo: “Artemision in Museum” by_[_Nikos Kitsakis_](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Nubero)_._

![Image 33: Jockey of Artemision](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/jockey-artemision.webp)

### Jockey of Artemision

Divers recovered this Hellenistic sculpture from the same shipwreck as the Zeus/Poseidon bronze. The bronze rider, dating to around **140 BC**, shows a young boy riding a galloping horse bareback and leaning into the animal's stride with the tension of a race's final stretch. Conservators reassembled both pieces from fragments after the underwater rescue, and they now occupy **Room 34**.

_Photo: “Jockey of Artemision” by_[_Nikos Kitsakis_](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Nubero).

![Image 34: Thera frescoes](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/antelopes-thera.webp)

### Thera frescoes

Volcanic ash from the Thera eruption around **1600 BC** preserved the wall paintings from the Bronze Age settlement of Akrotiri on Santorini. The set includes the _Spring_ fresco with its lilies and swallows, the _Fisherman_ holding two strings of catch, and the two _Boxing Boys_. Together they form one of the earliest surviving examples of large-scale wall painting in Europe and fill a dedicated gallery on the upper floor.

_Photo: “The Antelopes Fresco, from Akrotiri, Thera (Santorini), Minoan Civilization, 16th Century BC, National Archaeological Museum of Athens (14115163145)” by_[_Carole Raddato_](https://www.flickr.com/people/41523983@N08)_/_[_Butko_](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usuario:Butko)_._

### How to get

The museum sits at **44 Patission Street** in the Exarcheia district, north of Omonia Square.

The closest metro stop is **Victoria Station on Line 1 (Green)**, about a 7-minute walk along Heyden Street. **Omonia Station on Lines 1 and 2** lies a 10-minute walk to the south. Bus lines **224, 608, A7, and 622** stop at Polytechneio or Museio outside the entrance, while trolley buses **2, 3, 5, 11, and 15** follow Patission Street past the building.

![Image 38: National Archaelogica Museum of Athens](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/national-archaelogical-museum-of-athens-entrance.webp)

### Entrances

The museum has two entrances:

1.   The **main entrance** stands at **44 Patission Street**, behind a wide neoclassical staircase flanked by Doric columns, and handles standard visits with the security check, ticket desk, and cloakroom inside.
2.   A second, **accessible entrance** opens on **Vassileos Herakleiou Street** along the building's side, reached either by a ramp from the front esplanade or from the pavement, and connects to the elevators that serve the basement and upper floor.

## What should you know before visiting the Athens Archaeological Museum?

*   **Arrive early to beat the crowds:** doors open at 8:00 in summer and 8:30 in winter, and the first two hours are the quietest stretch. Tuesday afternoons, when the museum opens at 13:00, also offer a calm window for those who prefer a slow start.
*   **Plan for two to three hours inside:** five permanent collections spread across two floors and roughly 8,000 square metres of galleries, so even a focused visit takes time. The Mycenaean and Cycladic wings tend to absorb half of that slot for first-time visitors.
*   **Wear comfortable shoes:** marble floors run the full length of the building, and no shortcuts connect the prehistoric, sculpture, and bronze wings. Benches inside the galleries are sparse, so plan rest stops at the central atrium or the café.
*   **Use the cloakroom for bags:** backpacks and large bags must go to the entrance cloakroom, which is free of charge. Small purses, camera bags, and water bottles can stay with the visitor in the galleries.
*   **Photography is allowed without flash:** tripods, selfie sticks, and professional rigs are not permitted, and some temporary exhibitions restrict photography. Signs at the entrance of each gallery flag any extra rules in force that day.
*   **Pick up the floor plan at the desk:** the information desk hands out a free map of the main rooms and masterpieces. The Antikythera Mechanism (Room 38), Mask of Agamemnon (Room 4), and Artemision Bronze (Room 15) are easy to miss without it.
*   **Pair the museum with the Epigraphic Museum:** the neighbouring Epigraphic Museum stands on the same block and tends to be quieter. A half day covers both with time to spare.
*   **Accessibility is built in:** wheelchair loans, accessible restrooms, elevators, and the Vassileos Herakleiou Street ramp cover the whole building. The information desk provides tactile materials and a list of 20 sculptures suitable for tactile exploration on request.

## FAQs about the National Archaeological Museum of Athens

#### What is included in a ticket to the National Archaeological Museum?

The standard ticket grants access to **all five permanent collections** (Prehistoric Antiquities, Sculpture, Vases and Minor Arts, Bronze Works, and Egyptian and Eastern Antiquities) across the museum's two floors and basement.

#### How long does a visit to the museum take?

**Most visitors spend two to three hours inside**. A first visit focused on the headline pieces (Mask of Agamemnon, Antikythera Mechanism, Artemision Bronze, Thera frescoes, and Cycladic figurines) takes around 90 minutes. The full sweep of 11,000 exhibits across two floors fills half a day for visitors who want to explore at a slower pace.

#### When is the best time of day to visit?

**The first two hours after opening are the calmest**, especially in summer when the museum stays open until 20:00. Tuesday afternoons, with the late 13:00 opening, see lighter foot traffic, while late mornings between 11:00 and 13:00 tend to be the busiest stretch for tour groups. **Evenings after 18:00 in summer are another quiet window**.

#### Is the National Archaeological Museum wheelchair accessible?

**Yes**, the museum has a dedicated accessible entrance on Vassileos Herakleiou Street with a ramp leading inside, and elevators serve the basement and first floor. Loaner wheelchairs, accessible restrooms, and seating areas cover the building, and the information desk provides a list of 20 sculptures suitable for tactile exploration by visually impaired visitors.

#### How do I reach the museum from the city centre?

From **Syntagma Square**, a short metro transfer reaches Victoria Station on Line 1 (Green), about a 7-minute walk from the entrance along Heyden Street. The same trip on foot takes around 20 minutes via **Stadiou or Panepistimiou streets**. Buses 224 and 608 stop opposite the museum at the Polytechneio stop on Patission Street, and taxis recognise the museum by its Greek name, _Ethniko Archaiologiko Mouseio_.

#### Can children visit the museum?

**Yes, children of all ages are welcome**. The wide hallways take strollers without issue, and the restrooms include baby-changing facilities. The Cycladic figurines, Egyptian Collection, and Mycenaean gold tend to draw the most attention from younger visitors, and the information desk hands out a family-friendly map at the entrance.

## What can you see inside the museum?

Six highlights stand out from the rest of the works:

Mask of Agamemnon Antikythera Mechanism Artemision Bronze Jockey of Artemision Thera frescoes

![Image 30: mask of agamemnon](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/mask-of-agamemnon.webp)

### Mask of Agamemnon

Heinrich Schliemann unearthed the gold funerary mask at Mycenae in 1876, inside Grave Circle A. It dates to **1550-1500 BC**, three centuries before the Trojan War, and most likely covered the face of a Mycenaean ruler whose identity remains unknown. Hammered from a single sheet of gold, the portrait sits at the centre of the museum's Mycenaean collection in **Room 4**.

![Image 31: antikythera mechanism](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/antikythera-mechanism.webp)

### Antikythera Mechanism

Divers recovered the geared bronze device in 1901 from a shipwreck off the island of Antikythera, and it dates between **150 and 100 BC**. Researchers consider it the earliest known analog computer: more than 30 interlocking gears tracked astronomical positions, predicted lunar phases and eclipses, and timed the cycle of athletic festivals. The main fragment and several smaller pieces sit in **Room 38**, alongside digital reconstructions that show the mechanism in motion.

_Photo: “Antikythera Mechanism - National Archaeological Museum, Athens by Joy of Museum” by_[_Joyofmuseums_](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Joyofmuseums).

![Image 32: Artemision in Bronze](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/artemision.webp)

### Artemision Bronze of Zeus or Poseidon

Fishermen hauled the **2.09-metre bronze figure** from the seabed off Cape Artemision in 1928, and it is one of the few surviving large bronzes from early Classical sculpture. Scholars still debate whether it depicts Zeus poised to hurl a thunderbolt or Poseidon brandishing a trident, since the original attribute did not survive. The balanced stance, anatomical precision, and outstretched arms anchor **Room 15**.

_Photo: “Artemision in Museum” by_[_Nikos Kitsakis_](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Nubero)_._

![Image 33: Jockey of Artemision](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/jockey-artemision.webp)

### Jockey of Artemision

Divers recovered this Hellenistic sculpture from the same shipwreck as the Zeus/Poseidon bronze. The bronze rider, dating to around **140 BC**, shows a young boy riding a galloping horse bareback and leaning into the animal's stride with the tension of a race's final stretch. Conservators reassembled both pieces from fragments after the underwater rescue, and they now occupy **Room 34**.

_Photo: “Jockey of Artemision” by_[_Nikos Kitsakis_](https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/User:Nubero).

![Image 34: Thera frescoes](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/antelopes-thera.webp)

### Thera frescoes

Volcanic ash from the Thera eruption around **1600 BC** preserved the wall paintings from the Bronze Age settlement of Akrotiri on Santorini. The set includes the _Spring_ fresco with its lilies and swallows, the _Fisherman_ holding two strings of catch, and the two _Boxing Boys_. Together they form one of the earliest surviving examples of large-scale wall painting in Europe and fill a dedicated gallery on the upper floor.

_Photo: “The Antelopes Fresco, from Akrotiri, Thera (Santorini), Minoan Civilization, 16th Century BC, National Archaeological Museum of Athens (14115163145)” by_[_Carole Raddato_](https://www.flickr.com/people/41523983@N08)_/_[_Butko_](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Usuario:Butko)_._

### Opening hours

The museum operates on two seasonal schedules:

*   **Winter season (from Νovember 16th, 2025 to May 3rd, 2026):**
    *   Wednesday – Monday: 08:30 – 15:30 (last admission: 15:00).

    *   Wednesday – Monday: 08:00 – 20:00 (last admission: 19:30).

Last admission is **30 minutes before closing**, and the ticket desk closes at the same time year-round.

![Image 36: Best time to visit Athens](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/best-time-visit-athens.webp)

### Closing days & special dates

The Athens Archaeological Museum closes on six fixed dates each year:

*   **1 January** (New Year's Day)
*   **25 March** (Greek Independence Day)
*   **1 May** (Labour Day)
*   **Orthodox Easter Sunday**
*   **25 December** (Christmas Day)
*   **26 December** (Synaxis of the Mother of God)

![Image 37: How to get](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/national-archaelogical-museum-location-map.webp)

### How to get

The museum sits at **44 Patission Street** in the Exarcheia district, north of Omonia Square.

The closest metro stop is **Victoria Station on Line 1 (Green)**, about a 7-minute walk along Heyden Street. **Omonia Station on Lines 1 and 2** lies a 10-minute walk to the south. Bus lines **224, 608, A7, and 622** stop at Polytechneio or Museio outside the entrance, while trolley buses **2, 3, 5, 11, and 15** follow Patission Street past the building.

![Image 38: National Archaelogica Museum of Athens](https://cdn.ticketdoor.com/national-archaelogical-museum-of-athens-entrance.webp)

### Entrances

The museum has two entrances:

1.   The **main entrance** stands at **44 Patission Street**, behind a wide neoclassical staircase flanked by Doric columns, and handles standard visits with the security check, ticket desk, and cloakroom inside.
2.   A second, **accessible entrance** opens on **Vassileos Herakleiou Street** along the building's side, reached either by a ramp from the front esplanade or from the pavement, and connects to the elevators that serve the basement and upper floor.

## What should you know before visiting the Athens Archaeological Museum?

*   **Arrive early to beat the crowds:** doors open at 8:00 in summer and 8:30 in winter, and the first two hours are the quietest stretch. Tuesday afternoons, when the museum opens at 13:00, also offer a calm window for those who prefer a slow start.
*   **Plan for two to three hours inside:** five permanent collections spread across two floors and roughly 8,000 square metres of galleries, so even a focused visit takes time. The Mycenaean and Cycladic wings tend to absorb half of that slot for first-time visitors.
*   **Wear comfortable shoes:** marble floors run the full length of the building, and no shortcuts connect the prehistoric, sculpture, and bronze wings. Benches inside the galleries are sparse, so plan rest stops at the central atrium or the café.
*   **Use the cloakroom for bags:** backpacks and large bags must go to the entrance cloakroom, which is free of charge. Small purses, camera bags, and water bottles can stay with the visitor in the galleries.
*   **Photography is allowed without flash:** tripods, selfie sticks, and professional rigs are not permitted, and some temporary exhibitions restrict photography. Signs at the entrance of each gallery flag any extra rules in force that day.
*   **Pick up the floor plan at the desk:** the information desk hands out a free map of the main rooms and masterpieces. The Antikythera Mechanism (Room 38), Mask of Agamemnon (Room 4), and Artemision Bronze (Room 15) are easy to miss without it.
*   **Pair the museum with the Epigraphic Museum:** the neighbouring Epigraphic Museum stands on the same block and tends to be quieter. A half day covers both with time to spare.
*   **Accessibility is built in:** wheelchair loans, accessible restrooms, elevators, and the Vassileos Herakleiou Street ramp cover the whole building. The information desk provides tactile materials and a list of 20 sculptures suitable for tactile exploration on request.

## FAQs about the National Archaeological Museum of Athens

#### What is included in a ticket to the National Archaeological Museum?

The standard ticket grants access to **all five permanent collections** (Prehistoric Antiquities, Sculpture, Vases and Minor Arts, Bronze Works, and Egyptian and Eastern Antiquities) across the museum's two floors and basement.

#### How long does a visit to the museum take?

**Most visitors spend two to three hours inside**. A first visit focused on the headline pieces (Mask of Agamemnon, Antikythera Mechanism, Artemision Bronze, Thera frescoes, and Cycladic figurines) takes around 90 minutes. The full sweep of 11,000 exhibits across two floors fills half a day for visitors who want to explore at a slower pace.

#### When is the best time of day to visit?

**The first two hours after opening are the calmest**, especially in summer when the museum stays open until 20:00. Tuesday afternoons, with the late 13:00 opening, see lighter foot traffic, while late mornings between 11:00 and 13:00 tend to be the busiest stretch for tour groups. **Evenings after 18:00 in summer are another quiet window**.

#### Is the National Archaeological Museum wheelchair accessible?

**Yes**, the museum has a dedicated accessible entrance on Vassileos Herakleiou Street with a ramp leading inside, and elevators serve the basement and first floor. Loaner wheelchairs, accessible restrooms, and seating areas cover the building, and the information desk provides a list of 20 sculptures suitable for tactile exploration by visually impaired visitors.

#### How do I reach the museum from the city centre?

From **Syntagma Square**, a short metro transfer reaches Victoria Station on Line 1 (Green), about a 7-minute walk from the entrance along Heyden Street. The same trip on foot takes around 20 minutes via **Stadiou or Panepistimiou streets**. Buses 224 and 608 stop opposite the museum at the Polytechneio stop on Patission Street, and taxis recognise the museum by its Greek name, _Ethniko Archaiologiko Mouseio_.

#### Can children visit the museum?

**Yes, children of all ages are welcome**. The wide hallways take strollers without issue, and the restrooms include baby-changing facilities. The Cycladic figurines, Egyptian Collection, and Mycenaean gold tend to draw the most attention from younger visitors, and the information desk hands out a family-friendly map at the entrance.

# National Archaeological Museum of Athens: the complete guide — 12 must-see exhibits, tickets, hours, café

📅 30 March 2026 · updated 13 September 2026⏱️ 15 min read❤️ Kathy

[B](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/ "Blog")›[Museums & Sights](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/museums/)›National Archaeological Museum: the complete guide

 The National Archaeological Museum is the largest museum in Greece and one of the most important museums of antiquities in the world: more than 11,000 exhibits across 8,000 m², from the Neolithic era to late antiquity. It is also the museum closest to Angel Athens — an 8-minute walk from Ioulianou 50. In this guide you'll find the 12 exhibits you shouldn't miss (with room numbers), three ready-made routes depending on your time, 2026 hours and tickets, directions (including wheelchair access), the café in the garden and a video tour to get a feel for the place before you go.

## 🏛️ The building and the garden

The museum occupies the imposing neoclassical building at **44 Patission (28is Oktovriou) Street**, between Victoria and Omonia, right next to the Polytechnic. The foundations were laid in 1866 on land donated by Eleni Tositsa, with funds from the Bernardakis family of St Petersburg, designs by Ludwig Lange and the final façade by Ernst Ziller. It opened its doors in 1889 and was extended eastwards in 1932–1939. In front of it stretches the garden with its palm trees and flower beds — one of the loveliest "courtyards" in Athens, where Polytechnic students and locals sit in the afternoons.

## 🧭 Before you go in: how the museum is laid out

The museum is far too big for a casual stroll. You can easily spend half a day there and leave feeling you've only seen the beginning. It helps to know the logic of the building: on the **ground floor** are the Prehistoric Antiquities (rooms 3–6, directly opposite the entrance), Sculpture (rooms 7–35, in a loop around the building), the Bronzes (36–39) and the Egyptian Collection (40–41). On the **first floor** are the Thera frescoes (room 48), the Vase and Minor Arts Collection (49–63) and the Cypriot Collection (64).

Tip: start with the **Prehistoric Antiquities**. That's where the Mask of "Agamemnon", the Mycenaean finds and the Cycladic figurines are. Early in the morning the route is usually calmer and you can linger a little longer in front of the star pieces. Pick up the map at the entrance (or download the [floor plans](https://www.namuseum.gr/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/EAM_KATOPSEIS.pdf) to your phone) — the room numbers below follow the official numbering.

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss

### 1. The Mask of "Agamemnon"

📍 Room 4 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · c. 1550–1500 BC

Heinrich Schliemann found it in a shaft grave at Mycenae in 1876 and immediately linked it to Agamemnon. The dating, however, places it about three centuries before the Trojan War as we know it from the epic tradition. The name stuck, but the mask is more interesting when you see it as a Mycenaean funerary object: thin gold sheet, closed eyes, a face that looks more like a ritual image than a portrait. In the same room, look at the other, less famous gold masks and the swords with gold inlay — the comparison says a lot.

### 2. The royal tombs of Mycenae and the Vapheio Cups

📍 Rooms 3–4 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · 16th–15th c. BC

In the same rooms you'll see gold cups, daggers with inlaid hunting scenes, libation vessels, seal stones and the famous "Warrior Vase" — objects that show wealth, technical mastery and contacts with the whole eastern Mediterranean of the Bronze Age. The two **Vapheio Cups**, with scenes of wild bulls being captured in gold relief, were found in a tholos tomb in Laconia and are considered among the finest examples of prehistoric Aegean metalwork. Take your time: the details are tiny.

### 3. Cycladic figurines and the "Harpist" of Keros

📍 Room 6 · Ground floor · Cycladic Collection · 3200–2000 BC

The marble Cycladic figurines are small, austere and far more sophisticated than they look at first glance — it's no accident that they inspired Modigliani, Brancusi and Picasso. Look for the **"Harpist"**, a seated male figure playing a triangular harp, and the large female figurine from Amorgos, 1.5 metres tall. This room is a good, quiet breather before you move on to the sculpture.

### 4. The Akrotiri frescoes from Thera

📍 Room 48 · First floor · Thera Collection · c. 1600 BC

### Akrotiri on Thera: the "Pompeii of the Aegean"

The eruption of the Thera volcano buried the prehistoric town of Akrotiri under volcanic ash, preserving wall paintings of unusual vividness. The "Boxing Children", the "Antelopes" and the "Spring" fresco with its lilies and swallows show an Aegean world that is colourful, maritime and far more familiar than you'd expect from the Bronze Age. The room is dark and cool — a perfect stop on hot days.

### 5. Linear B tablets

📍 Room 5 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · 1450–1200 BC

Small clay tablets, some no bigger than a credit card, inscribed with the earliest deciphered Greek script: a syllabic system used for accounting records in the Mycenaean palaces of Pylos, Mycenae and Thebes. They survived by pure accident: the palaces burned, the unbaked clay was fired, and the bureaucratic notes endured. Michael Ventris's decipherment in 1952 pushed the history of the Greek language back by about 700 years.

### 6. The Kouros of Sounion

📍 Room 8 · Ground floor · Archaic Sculpture · c. 600 BC

As soon as you pass from the Prehistoric galleries into Sculpture, the three-metre Kouros of Sounion shows the Archaic figure in its strictest form: frontal, upright, with the familiar "archaic smile" and a body organised in clean lines. It was set up as a votive offering in the sanctuary of Poseidon at Sounion. Keep it in mind when you reach the bronzes of the following rooms — the difference says a lot about how Greek sculpture evolved in just 150 years.

### 7. The Artemision Bronze (Zeus or Poseidon)

📍 Room 15 · Ground floor · Classical Sculpture · c. 460 BC

Raised from a shipwreck off Cape Artemision in Euboea in 1926–1928. The bronze body, 2.09 m tall, is caught in the moment of throwing — the open hand once held a thunderbolt or a trident, which is why you'll see it called both Zeus and Poseidon. Its value is enormous for one simple reason: original Greek bronzes rarely survive, because most were melted down for their metal in later centuries. It is the star of room 15 and the most photographed statue in the museum.

### 8. The Marathon Boy

📍 Room 28 · Ground floor · Classical bronzes · c. 340–330 BC

Another original bronze, from the sea off Marathon, where it was found in 1925. The young athlete stands with a slight tilt and originally held something that hasn't survived — perhaps a disc or a lamp. The attribution to the circle of Praxiteles has been much debated, without being certain. See it after the Kouros of Sounion: the distance between the two works shows how much the relationship between body and movement had changed. In the same room stands the bronze **Antikythera Ephebe**.

### 9. The Jockey of Artemision

📍 Room 21 · Ground floor · Hellenistic Sculpture · c. 140 BC

From the same shipwreck as the Zeus/Poseidon comes the most "cinematic" work in the museum: a small boy, possibly an African rider, on a horse galloping with legs outstretched. The fragments were raised in two phases (1928 and 1936–37) and the group was only reassembled in 1972. The horse is 2.90 m tall and the child just 84 cm — the contrast in scale makes the movement even more intense. It's the piece you'll look at longest in room 21.

### 10. The Antikythera Mechanism

📍 Room 38 · Ground floor · Metalwork Collection · 2nd–1st c. BC

The Antikythera Mechanism is one of the main reasons to visit the museum — the **oldest known analogue computer** in the world. The 82 fragments of the geared bronze device were raised from a shipwreck off Antikythera by sponge divers from Symi in 1900–1901; it calculated the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, eclipses and the dates of the Olympic Games. Nothing of comparable complexity was made for more than a thousand years afterwards. Don't settle for a first glance: the reconstruction models and the video in the room help enormously in understanding what you're looking at.

### 11. The bronze "Philosopher" of Antikythera

📍 Room 28 · Ground floor · Hellenistic bronzes · c. 240–200 BC

From the same shipwreck comes the so-called "Philosopher": a head with unkempt hair, a beard, wrinkles and a gaze that follows you. We don't need to know for certain whom it depicts (the Cynic Bion of Borysthenes and others have been proposed) to understand its significance. Hellenistic art here leaves behind the ideal youth of the Classical period and looks at the face with far greater psychological intensity.

### 12. The Dipylon Amphora

📍 Room 49 · First floor · Vase Collection · c. 760–750 BC

Upstairs, at the start of the Vase Collection, the Dipylon Amphora (1.55 m tall) shows Geometric art on a monumental scale: bands of meanders, rows of animals and, on the neck, a scene of a dead woman laid out with mourners clutching their heads. It served as a grave marker in the Dipylon cemetery at Kerameikos. It's a good final stop, because it takes you away from the "big names" and reminds you how powerful pottery can be.

## 🎁 Bonus: 8 more works if you have time

*   **The Kouros of Aristodikos** (room 13, c. 500 BC) — the last step before the Classical style.
*   **The Great Eleusinian Relief** (room 14, c. 440 BC) — Demeter, Persephone and Triptolemos in high Classical style.
*   **The Grave Stele of Hegeso** (room 18, c. 410 BC) — the most tender funerary monument in Athens.
*   **The Varvakeion Athena** (room 20) — the most faithful copy of Phidias' gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos.
*   **Aphrodite, Pan and Eros** (room 30, c. 100 BC) — the museum's most humorous sculpture, from Delos.
*   **The Poseidon of Melos** (room 30, c. 130 BC) — a monumental Hellenistic deity.
*   **The Egyptian Collection** (rooms 40–41) — mummies, sarcophagi and one of the most important Egyptian collections outside Egypt, from the Dimitriou (1880) and Rostovitz (1904) donations.
*   **The Cypriot Collection** (room 64, first floor) — around 850 works, the richest Cypriot collection outside Cyprus.

## 📜 The museum's history — and how the statues were saved in the war

The National Archaeological Museum is the first museum founded by the Greek state, in **1829**, initially on Aegina, then the capital. It moved to Athens in 1834 and passed through several buildings (the Theseion, Hadrian's Library, the Tower of the Winds, the University) before getting its own home on Patission Street. The collections grew rapidly with the excavations of the 19th century — Mycenae, Sounion, Epidaurus, Delos, Antikythera — and in 1932–1939 the east wing by G. Nomikos was added.

### November 1940: the museum "buries" its treasures

A few days after Greece entered the Second World War, the museum's management was ordered to hide all the antiquities. Within six months, archaeologists, conservators, guards and workmen laboured day and night: the marble statues were buried in **trenches dug into the floors of the galleries themselves** and covered with sand and concrete; the bronzes and pottery were packed into 57 crates hidden in the cave of Enneakrounos and the so-called "Prison of Socrates" on Philopappos Hill, while the gold treasures of Mycenae went down into the vaults of the Bank of Greece. During the Occupation the Germans demanded that 103 statues be re-erected for their soldiers — director Christos Karouzos and Semni Karouzou refused. In December 1944, during the Dekemvriana fighting, mortar shells hit the roof; the buried marbles were untouched. Unearthing began in June 1946, and the poet George Seferis, who watched it, spoke of "a dance of resurrection". The museum gradually reopened from 1947.

The 1999 earthquake caused damage and led to the major renovation of 2002–2004 ahead of the Olympic Games. The collections reopened one by one until 2009, with new displays and lighting. The Numismatic Museum, which had been housed here, moved to the Iliou Melathron, Schliemann's mansion on Panepistimiou Street. A large underground extension beneath the garden, designed by David Chipperfield, has been announced for the coming years — when complete, the museum will almost double its exhibition space.

E-tickets are issued at [tickets.hh.gr](https://tickets.hh.gr/en/venues/national-archaeological-museum) (Hellenic Heritage) — there are no time slots, the ticket is valid for the day you choose and it saves you the queue at the desk. There are also physical ticket desks at the entrance. The ticket is not included in the Acropolis combined ticket (see our [guide to the combined ticket](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/museums/athens-combined-ticket-worth-it/)).

## ♿ Accessibility

*   **Accessible entrance:** a separate entrance on the **Vas. Irakleiou Street** side (the side street to the right of the façade). You reach it either by ramp from the front garden or directly from the Vas. Irakleiou pavement. The main entrance has steps.
*   A **lift** connects the ground and first floors (priority for visitors with mobility impairments). The ground-floor galleries are level, with only a few small changes in height.
*   A **wheelchair** can be requested from the entrance staff, subject to availability — best to phone ahead (+30 213 214 4800).
*   **Accessible toilets** on the ground floor. Free WiFi and a cloakroom for backpacks (large backpacks must be checked in).
*   The museum offers a [digital virtual tour](https://www.namuseum.gr/en/digital-virtual-tour-for-persons-with-mobility-impairment-or-hard-of-hearing-individuals-in-the-context-of-the-national-archaeological-museum-action-plan-for-people-with-disabilities/) for people with mobility or hearing impairments, and organises touch tours for blind visitors by arrangement.
*   **Admission:** free for disabled visitors and one companion, on presentation of the relevant document.

One of the best-kept secrets in the area: the museum café operates in the inner garden-patio, with tables under the trees, among ancient architectural fragments and planting renewed with 700 new plant species. Best of all: **entry to the café is free, no ticket required** — you go in through the secondary entrance to the right of the main staircase. ## 🛍️ The museum shop

The museum shop reopened, renovated and under new management, in August 2025 and keeps the museum's days and hours. You'll find the museum's official publications and catalogues, faithful replicas of exhibits (Cycladic figurines, the Mask of Agamemnon in various sizes, the Antikythera Mechanism), jewellery inspired by the collection and quality souvenirs — a far better choice than the tourist shops of Plaka for a gift with meaning.

## ⏳ How much time to allow — 3 ready-made routes

#### 90 minutes — the highlights

Mask of Agamemnon (room 4) → Cycladic (6) → Kouros of Sounion (8) → Zeus/Poseidon (15) → Jockey (21) → Marathon Boy (28) → Antikythera Mechanism (38). All on the ground floor, in a logical order.

#### 3 hours — recommended

All 12 exhibits at a relaxed pace, plus the Sculpture bonus, the Thera frescoes (48) and the vases on the first floor. Coffee break in the garden halfway through.

#### 5+ hours — the full museum

All six collections, including Egyptian and Cypriot, with lunch in the garden. Or split it over two visits — you're staying 8 minutes away.

## 💡 10 tips from Kathy

1.   **Go early or on a Tuesday afternoon.** Cruise-ship groups arrive between 10:30 and 13:00. At 08:30 you'll have the Mask almost to yourself.
2.   **Start with the Prehistoric galleries (rooms 3–6)** and continue clockwise through Sculpture — that way you see the art in chronological order.
3.   **Download the floor plans** (PDF from namuseum.gr) before you go in. The building is a labyrinth.
4.   **Photography without flash is allowed** for personal use. No tripods or selfie sticks. Don't pose "imitating" the statues — staff will stop you.
5.   **Large backpacks go to the cloakroom** (free). Take only your phone and water with you.
6.   **Buy an e-ticket** at tickets.hh.gr to skip the queue, especially April–October.
7.   **The café needs no ticket** — you can go just for a coffee in the garden, even on days you're not visiting the museum.
8.   **With children:** aim for the Mechanism, the Jockey, the bronzes and the Egyptian mummies. One hour, then out for ice cream.
9.   **Combine it** with a walk in [Pedion tou Areos park](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/our-neighborhood/pedion-tou-areos-park-victoria-guide/) (5 minutes) or along [historic Patission Street](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/our-neighborhood/patision-street-historic-axis-museum-shops/).
10.   **Check the temporary exhibitions** — they're often excellent and included in the ticket.

## ❓ Frequently asked questions

### How much is a ticket to the National Archaeological Museum?

€20 full and €10 reduced, all year round. Free for children and young people up to 25 from EU countries, disabled visitors with a companion, and for everyone on free-admission days (6 March, 18 April, 18 May, last weekend of September, 28 October, 1st and 3rd Sundays from November to March).

### What are the opening hours?

In winter (mid-November to early May) Wednesday–Monday 08:30–15:30 and Tuesday 13:00–20:00. In summer (May to mid-November) Wednesday–Monday 08:00–20:00 and Tuesday 13:00–20:00. Last admission 30 minutes before closing. Closed 1 Jan, 25 Mar, 1 May, Easter Sunday, 25–26 Dec.

### How long does a visit take?

90 minutes for the ground-floor highlights, 3 hours for a full visit including the first floor, 5+ hours if you want to see all six collections. If you're staying nearby, it's more pleasant to split it over two days.

### Is it worth the trip just for the Antikythera Mechanism?

For anyone interested in the history of science or technology, yes. It isn't the most spectacular exhibit at first glance, but the more you understand what it did, the more impressive it becomes. The reconstruction models in room 38 help a lot.

### Can you visit with children?

Yes, but keep the route short. For younger children pick a few exhibits with a clear image: the Mechanism, the Jockey of Artemision, the Cycladic harpist, the Egyptian mummies and the bronzes. The garden café is ideal for a break. If you try to see the whole museum, they'll tire quickly.

### Is it wheelchair accessible?

Yes. There's a separate accessible entrance on Vas. Irakleiou Street with a ramp, a lift to the first floor and accessible toilets. Admission is free for the disabled visitor and their companion.

### Is photography allowed?

Yes, without flash, for personal use. Tripods, professional equipment and commercial use require a permit. Posing in imitation of the exhibits is not allowed.

### Can I go to the café without a ticket?

Yes. Entry to the café and garden is free, via the secondary entrance to the right of the main staircase, during museum hours.

### Is it closer to the Acropolis or to Omonia?

Omonia — about 12 minutes on foot north of the metro station, and 8 minutes from Victoria station. From the Acropolis it's a 30–35 minute walk through the centre, or metro Line 2 from Akropoli to Omonia (3 stops).

# National Archaeological Museum of Athens: the complete guide — 12 must-see exhibits, tickets, hours, café

📅 30 March 2026 · updated 13 September 2026⏱️ 15 min read❤️ Kathy

[B](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/ "Blog")›[Museums & Sights](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/museums/)›National Archaeological Museum: the complete guide

 The National Archaeological Museum is the largest museum in Greece and one of the most important museums of antiquities in the world: more than 11,000 exhibits across 8,000 m², from the Neolithic era to late antiquity. It is also the museum closest to Angel Athens — an 8-minute walk from Ioulianou 50. In this guide you'll find the 12 exhibits you shouldn't miss (with room numbers), three ready-made routes depending on your time, 2026 hours and tickets, directions (including wheelchair access), the café in the garden and a video tour to get a feel for the place before you go.

## 🏛️ The building and the garden

The museum occupies the imposing neoclassical building at **44 Patission (28is Oktovriou) Street**, between Victoria and Omonia, right next to the Polytechnic. The foundations were laid in 1866 on land donated by Eleni Tositsa, with funds from the Bernardakis family of St Petersburg, designs by Ludwig Lange and the final façade by Ernst Ziller. It opened its doors in 1889 and was extended eastwards in 1932–1939. In front of it stretches the garden with its palm trees and flower beds — one of the loveliest "courtyards" in Athens, where Polytechnic students and locals sit in the afternoons.

## 🧭 Before you go in: how the museum is laid out

The museum is far too big for a casual stroll. You can easily spend half a day there and leave feeling you've only seen the beginning. It helps to know the logic of the building: on the **ground floor** are the Prehistoric Antiquities (rooms 3–6, directly opposite the entrance), Sculpture (rooms 7–35, in a loop around the building), the Bronzes (36–39) and the Egyptian Collection (40–41). On the **first floor** are the Thera frescoes (room 48), the Vase and Minor Arts Collection (49–63) and the Cypriot Collection (64).

Tip: start with the **Prehistoric Antiquities**. That's where the Mask of "Agamemnon", the Mycenaean finds and the Cycladic figurines are. Early in the morning the route is usually calmer and you can linger a little longer in front of the star pieces. Pick up the map at the entrance (or download the [floor plans](https://www.namuseum.gr/wp-content/uploads/2018/10/EAM_KATOPSEIS.pdf) to your phone) — the room numbers below follow the official numbering.

## 🏆 The 12 exhibits you must not miss

### 1. The Mask of "Agamemnon"

📍 Room 4 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · c. 1550–1500 BC

Heinrich Schliemann found it in a shaft grave at Mycenae in 1876 and immediately linked it to Agamemnon. The dating, however, places it about three centuries before the Trojan War as we know it from the epic tradition. The name stuck, but the mask is more interesting when you see it as a Mycenaean funerary object: thin gold sheet, closed eyes, a face that looks more like a ritual image than a portrait. In the same room, look at the other, less famous gold masks and the swords with gold inlay — the comparison says a lot.

### 2. The royal tombs of Mycenae and the Vapheio Cups

📍 Rooms 3–4 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · 16th–15th c. BC

In the same rooms you'll see gold cups, daggers with inlaid hunting scenes, libation vessels, seal stones and the famous "Warrior Vase" — objects that show wealth, technical mastery and contacts with the whole eastern Mediterranean of the Bronze Age. The two **Vapheio Cups**, with scenes of wild bulls being captured in gold relief, were found in a tholos tomb in Laconia and are considered among the finest examples of prehistoric Aegean metalwork. Take your time: the details are tiny.

### 3. Cycladic figurines and the "Harpist" of Keros

📍 Room 6 · Ground floor · Cycladic Collection · 3200–2000 BC

The marble Cycladic figurines are small, austere and far more sophisticated than they look at first glance — it's no accident that they inspired Modigliani, Brancusi and Picasso. Look for the **"Harpist"**, a seated male figure playing a triangular harp, and the large female figurine from Amorgos, 1.5 metres tall. This room is a good, quiet breather before you move on to the sculpture.

### 4. The Akrotiri frescoes from Thera

📍 Room 48 · First floor · Thera Collection · c. 1600 BC

### Akrotiri on Thera: the "Pompeii of the Aegean"

The eruption of the Thera volcano buried the prehistoric town of Akrotiri under volcanic ash, preserving wall paintings of unusual vividness. The "Boxing Children", the "Antelopes" and the "Spring" fresco with its lilies and swallows show an Aegean world that is colourful, maritime and far more familiar than you'd expect from the Bronze Age. The room is dark and cool — a perfect stop on hot days.

### 5. Linear B tablets

📍 Room 5 · Ground floor · Mycenaean Collection · 1450–1200 BC

Small clay tablets, some no bigger than a credit card, inscribed with the earliest deciphered Greek script: a syllabic system used for accounting records in the Mycenaean palaces of Pylos, Mycenae and Thebes. They survived by pure accident: the palaces burned, the unbaked clay was fired, and the bureaucratic notes endured. Michael Ventris's decipherment in 1952 pushed the history of the Greek language back by about 700 years.

### 6. The Kouros of Sounion

📍 Room 8 · Ground floor · Archaic Sculpture · c. 600 BC

As soon as you pass from the Prehistoric galleries into Sculpture, the three-metre Kouros of Sounion shows the Archaic figure in its strictest form: frontal, upright, with the familiar "archaic smile" and a body organised in clean lines. It was set up as a votive offering in the sanctuary of Poseidon at Sounion. Keep it in mind when you reach the bronzes of the following rooms — the difference says a lot about how Greek sculpture evolved in just 150 years.

### 7. The Artemision Bronze (Zeus or Poseidon)

📍 Room 15 · Ground floor · Classical Sculpture · c. 460 BC

Raised from a shipwreck off Cape Artemision in Euboea in 1926–1928. The bronze body, 2.09 m tall, is caught in the moment of throwing — the open hand once held a thunderbolt or a trident, which is why you'll see it called both Zeus and Poseidon. Its value is enormous for one simple reason: original Greek bronzes rarely survive, because most were melted down for their metal in later centuries. It is the star of room 15 and the most photographed statue in the museum.

### 8. The Marathon Boy

📍 Room 28 · Ground floor · Classical bronzes · c. 340–330 BC

Another original bronze, from the sea off Marathon, where it was found in 1925. The young athlete stands with a slight tilt and originally held something that hasn't survived — perhaps a disc or a lamp. The attribution to the circle of Praxiteles has been much debated, without being certain. See it after the Kouros of Sounion: the distance between the two works shows how much the relationship between body and movement had changed. In the same room stands the bronze **Antikythera Ephebe**.

### 9. The Jockey of Artemision

📍 Room 21 · Ground floor · Hellenistic Sculpture · c. 140 BC

From the same shipwreck as the Zeus/Poseidon comes the most "cinematic" work in the museum: a small boy, possibly an African rider, on a horse galloping with legs outstretched. The fragments were raised in two phases (1928 and 1936–37) and the group was only reassembled in 1972. The horse is 2.90 m tall and the child just 84 cm — the contrast in scale makes the movement even more intense. It's the piece you'll look at longest in room 21.

### 10. The Antikythera Mechanism

📍 Room 38 · Ground floor · Metalwork Collection · 2nd–1st c. BC

The Antikythera Mechanism is one of the main reasons to visit the museum — the **oldest known analogue computer** in the world. The 82 fragments of the geared bronze device were raised from a shipwreck off Antikythera by sponge divers from Symi in 1900–1901; it calculated the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets, eclipses and the dates of the Olympic Games. Nothing of comparable complexity was made for more than a thousand years afterwards. Don't settle for a first glance: the reconstruction models and the video in the room help enormously in understanding what you're looking at.

### 11. The bronze "Philosopher" of Antikythera

📍 Room 28 · Ground floor · Hellenistic bronzes · c. 240–200 BC

From the same shipwreck comes the so-called "Philosopher": a head with unkempt hair, a beard, wrinkles and a gaze that follows you. We don't need to know for certain whom it depicts (the Cynic Bion of Borysthenes and others have been proposed) to understand its significance. Hellenistic art here leaves behind the ideal youth of the Classical period and looks at the face with far greater psychological intensity.

### 12. The Dipylon Amphora

📍 Room 49 · First floor · Vase Collection · c. 760–750 BC

Upstairs, at the start of the Vase Collection, the Dipylon Amphora (1.55 m tall) shows Geometric art on a monumental scale: bands of meanders, rows of animals and, on the neck, a scene of a dead woman laid out with mourners clutching their heads. It served as a grave marker in the Dipylon cemetery at Kerameikos. It's a good final stop, because it takes you away from the "big names" and reminds you how powerful pottery can be.

## 🎁 Bonus: 8 more works if you have time

*   **The Kouros of Aristodikos** (room 13, c. 500 BC) — the last step before the Classical style.
*   **The Great Eleusinian Relief** (room 14, c. 440 BC) — Demeter, Persephone and Triptolemos in high Classical style.
*   **The Grave Stele of Hegeso** (room 18, c. 410 BC) — the most tender funerary monument in Athens.
*   **The Varvakeion Athena** (room 20) — the most faithful copy of Phidias' gold-and-ivory Athena Parthenos.
*   **Aphrodite, Pan and Eros** (room 30, c. 100 BC) — the museum's most humorous sculpture, from Delos.
*   **The Poseidon of Melos** (room 30, c. 130 BC) — a monumental Hellenistic deity.
*   **The Egyptian Collection** (rooms 40–41) — mummies, sarcophagi and one of the most important Egyptian collections outside Egypt, from the Dimitriou (1880) and Rostovitz (1904) donations.
*   **The Cypriot Collection** (room 64, first floor) — around 850 works, the richest Cypriot collection outside Cyprus.

## 📜 The museum's history — and how the statues were saved in the war

The National Archaeological Museum is the first museum founded by the Greek state, in **1829**, initially on Aegina, then the capital. It moved to Athens in 1834 and passed through several buildings (the Theseion, Hadrian's Library, the Tower of the Winds, the University) before getting its own home on Patission Street. The collections grew rapidly with the excavations of the 19th century — Mycenae, Sounion, Epidaurus, Delos, Antikythera — and in 1932–1939 the east wing by G. Nomikos was added.

### November 1940: the museum "buries" its treasures

A few days after Greece entered the Second World War, the museum's management was ordered to hide all the antiquities. Within six months, archaeologists, conservators, guards and workmen laboured day and night: the marble statues were buried in **trenches dug into the floors of the galleries themselves** and covered with sand and concrete; the bronzes and pottery were packed into 57 crates hidden in the cave of Enneakrounos and the so-called "Prison of Socrates" on Philopappos Hill, while the gold treasures of Mycenae went down into the vaults of the Bank of Greece. During the Occupation the Germans demanded that 103 statues be re-erected for their soldiers — director Christos Karouzos and Semni Karouzou refused. In December 1944, during the Dekemvriana fighting, mortar shells hit the roof; the buried marbles were untouched. Unearthing began in June 1946, and the poet George Seferis, who watched it, spoke of "a dance of resurrection". The museum gradually reopened from 1947.

The 1999 earthquake caused damage and led to the major renovation of 2002–2004 ahead of the Olympic Games. The collections reopened one by one until 2009, with new displays and lighting. The Numismatic Museum, which had been housed here, moved to the Iliou Melathron, Schliemann's mansion on Panepistimiou Street. A large underground extension beneath the garden, designed by David Chipperfield, has been announced for the coming years — when complete, the museum will almost double its exhibition space.

## ♿ Accessibility

*   **Accessible entrance:** a separate entrance on the **Vas. Irakleiou Street** side (the side street to the right of the façade). You reach it either by ramp from the front garden or directly from the Vas. Irakleiou pavement. The main entrance has steps.
*   A **lift** connects the ground and first floors (priority for visitors with mobility impairments). The ground-floor galleries are level, with only a few small changes in height.
*   A **wheelchair** can be requested from the entrance staff, subject to availability — best to phone ahead (+30 213 214 4800).
*   **Accessible toilets** on the ground floor. Free WiFi and a cloakroom for backpacks (large backpacks must be checked in).
*   The museum offers a [digital virtual tour](https://www.namuseum.gr/en/digital-virtual-tour-for-persons-with-mobility-impairment-or-hard-of-hearing-individuals-in-the-context-of-the-national-archaeological-museum-action-plan-for-people-with-disabilities/) for people with mobility or hearing impairments, and organises touch tours for blind visitors by arrangement.
*   **Admission:** free for disabled visitors and one companion, on presentation of the relevant document.

One of the best-kept secrets in the area: the museum café operates in the inner garden-patio, with tables under the trees, among ancient architectural fragments and planting renewed with 700 new plant species. Best of all: **entry to the café is free, no ticket required** — you go in through the secondary entrance to the right of the main staircase. It keeps museum hours, with extended hours in the summer months.

We wrote about the café in detail in [O Kipos tou Mouseiou: coffee in the garden of the National Archaeological Museum](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/food-and-cafes/o-kipos-tou-mouseiou-arxaiologiko-mouseio/).

## 🛍️ The museum shop

The museum shop reopened, renovated and under new management, in August 2025 and keeps the museum's days and hours. You'll find the museum's official publications and catalogues, faithful replicas of exhibits (Cycladic figurines, the Mask of Agamemnon in various sizes, the Antikythera Mechanism), jewellery inspired by the collection and quality souvenirs — a far better choice than the tourist shops of Plaka for a gift with meaning.

## ⏳ How much time to allow — 3 ready-made routes

#### 90 minutes — the highlights

Mask of Agamemnon (room 4) → Cycladic (6) → Kouros of Sounion (8) → Zeus/Poseidon (15) → Jockey (21) → Marathon Boy (28) → Antikythera Mechanism (38). All on the ground floor, in a logical order.

#### 3 hours — recommended

All 12 exhibits at a relaxed pace, plus the Sculpture bonus, the Thera frescoes (48) and the vases on the first floor. Coffee break in the garden halfway through.

#### 5+ hours — the full museum

All six collections, including Egyptian and Cypriot, with lunch in the garden. Or split it over two visits — you're staying 8 minutes away.

## 💡 10 tips from Kathy

1.   **Go early or on a Tuesday afternoon.** Cruise-ship groups arrive between 10:30 and 13:00. At 08:30 you'll have the Mask almost to yourself.
2.   **Start with the Prehistoric galleries (rooms 3–6)** and continue clockwise through Sculpture — that way you see the art in chronological order.
3.   **Download the floor plans** (PDF from namuseum.gr) before you go in. The building is a labyrinth.
4.   **Photography without flash is allowed** for personal use. No tripods or selfie sticks. Don't pose "imitating" the statues — staff will stop you.
5.   **Large backpacks go to the cloakroom** (free). Take only your phone and water with you.
6.   **Buy an e-ticket** at tickets.hh.gr to skip the queue, especially April–October.
7.   **The café needs no ticket** — you can go just for a coffee in the garden, even on days you're not visiting the museum.
8.   **With children:** aim for the Mechanism, the Jockey, the bronzes and the Egyptian mummies. One hour, then out for ice cream.
9.   **Combine it** with a walk in [Pedion tou Areos park](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/our-neighborhood/pedion-tou-areos-park-victoria-guide/) (5 minutes) or along [historic Patission Street](https://www.angelsathens.gr/en/blog/our-neighborhood/patision-street-historic-axis-museum-shops/).
10.   **Check the temporary exhibitions** — they're often excellent and included in the ticket.

## ❓ Frequently asked questions

### How much is a ticket to the National Archaeological Museum?

€20 full and €10 reduced, all year round. Free for children and young people up to 25 from EU countries, disabled visitors with a companion, and for everyone on free-admission days (6 March, 18 April, 18 May, last weekend of September, 28 October, 1st and 3rd Sundays from November to March).

### What are the opening hours?

In winter (mid-November to early May) Wednesday–Monday 08:30–15:30 and Tuesday 13:00–20:00. In summer (May to mid-November) Wednesday–Monday 08:00–20:00 and Tuesday 13:00–20:00. Last admission 30 minutes before closing. Closed 1 Jan, 25 Mar, 1 May, Easter Sunday, 25–26 Dec.

### How long does a visit take?

90 minutes for the ground-floor highlights, 3 hours for a full visit including the first floor, 5+ hours if you want to see all six collections. If you're staying nearby, it's more pleasant to split it over two days.

### Is it worth the trip just for the Antikythera Mechanism?

For anyone interested in the history of science or technology, yes. It isn't the most spectacular exhibit at first glance, but the more you understand what it did, the more impressive it becomes. The reconstruction models in room 38 help a lot.

### Can you visit with children?

Yes, but keep the route short. For younger children pick a few exhibits with a clear image: the Mechanism, the Jockey of Artemision, the Cycladic harpist, the Egyptian mummies and the bronzes. The garden café is ideal for a break. If you try to see the whole museum, they'll tire quickly.

### Is it wheelchair accessible?

Yes. There's a separate accessible entrance on Vas. Irakleiou Street with a ramp, a lift to the first floor and accessible toilets. Admission is free for the disabled visitor and their companion.

### Is photography allowed?

Yes, without flash, for personal use. Tripods, professional equipment and commercial use require a permit. Posing in imitation of the exhibits is not allowed.

### Can I go to the café without a ticket?

Yes. Entry to the café and garden is free, via the secondary entrance to the right of the main staircase, during museum hours.

### Is it closer to the Acropolis or to Omonia?

Omonia — about 12 minutes on foot north of the metro station, and 8 minutes from Victoria station. From the Acropolis it's a 30–35 minute walk through the centre, or metro Line 2 from Akropoli to Omonia (3 stops).
